title: Jana: the -li- slot for what's over
goal: Talk about what has already happened — the weekend, a trip, yesterday's weather — and negate it by swapping the slot, not the ending.
bekal: the negative: *-li-* becomes *-ku-* and the verb ending stays put
*nilikuwa* and *kulikuwa na* — I was, there was

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Wikendi ilikuwaje?
dialogs.intro: Monday morning on campus. Amina wants to know where Budi disappeared to for two days.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Habari za Jumatatu! Ulifanya nini wikendi?
lines.id: Happy Monday! What did you do at the weekend?
lines.literal: news of Monday! you-past-do what weekend?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I went to Bagamoyo with Juma.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Really? How did you get there?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tulipanda basi mapema. Safari ilichukua saa tatu.
lines.id: We took the bus early. The trip took three hours.
lines.literal: we-past-board bus early. journey it-past-take hours three.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tuliona bahari, majengo ya zamani, na soko kubwa.
lines.id: We saw the sea, old buildings, and a big market.
lines.literal: we-past-see sea, buildings of long-ago, and market big.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tulikula samaki wa kupaka ufuoni. Ilikuwa tamu sana!
lines.id: We had fish in coconut sauce on the beach. It was delicious!
lines.literal: we-past-eat fish of smearing on-beach. it-past-be sweet very!

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Hapa jana kulikuwa na mvua kubwa siku nzima.
lines.id: Here it rained heavily all day yesterday.
lines.literal: here yesterday there-past-be with rain big day whole.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Huko hakukuwa na mvua. Jua lilikuwa kali sana.
lines.id: There was no rain there. The sun was really strong.
lines.literal: there not-there-past-be with rain. sun it-past-be sharp very.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tulirudi usiku. Sikulala vizuri — nilichoka sana.
lines.id: We got back at night. I didn't sleep well — I was very tired.
lines.literal: we-past-return night. I-not-past-sleep well — I-past-tire very.

notes: **Vipi means "how" and goes at the end.** *Mlisafiri vipi?* (you traveled how?), *Ilikuwaje?* (how was it?). The second form glues the suffix *-je* straight onto the verb — same job, shorter.
**Huko means "there" for a place being talked about**, not one you can see. *Kule* is for a place you can point to. The same contrast as *hapo* and *pale* in unit 6.

**Bagamoyo is an old port town across from Zanzibar.** Its name means "lay down your heart" — from *bwaga* (lay down) and *moyo* (heart), a bitter legacy of its days as a slave-trade port. You'll meet *moyo* often: *moyo mkunjufu* (an open heart), *kwa moyo wote* (with all my heart).
**Siku nzima means "all day".** *-zima* means whole, complete: *mwaka mzima* (a whole year), *usiku kucha* (all night long). Note that *siku* is in the N class, so *-zima* becomes *nzima*.

**Samaki wa kupaka is Zanzibar's most famous dish**: grilled fish brushed with spiced coconut milk. *Kupaka* means to smear or brush on, and the linker *wa* marks the kind — just like *maji ya matunda* and *chai ya maziwa*.

grammars.title: The -li- slot: what's already over
body: To move into the past, you **change nothing but the middle slot**. The root stays whole, the subject prefix stays whole. Swap *-na-* for **-li-**, done.
after: One-syllable verbs keep their *ku-* exactly as in the present: *nilikula*, *nilikunywa*, *nilikuja*, *nilikwenda*, *nilikuwa*.
Noun-class prefixes work as usual: *safari ilichukua* (the trip took), *magari yalifika* (the cars arrived), *kitabu kilipotea* (the book got lost), *watoto walicheza* (the children played).
Swahili doesn't separate "I read" and "I have read" in this slot — *nilisoma* covers both. "Done, and the result still matters" belongs to the *-me-* slot, and that's next unit's business.

grammars.title: The negative: -li- becomes -ku-, the ending stays
body: This is where people slip most, yet the rule is actually easier than in the present: **the verb ending doesn't change at all**. Only the two front slots are swapped.
after: Note that this *-ku-* is **not** the filler *ku-* from unit 3, even though it sounds the same — it's the negative past slot. That's why short verbs don't double it: *nilikula* becomes *sikula*, not *sikukula*.

For **"was"** use *kuwa*: *nilikuwa mwanafunzi* (I was a student), *ilikuwa tamu* (it tasted great), *hakukuwa na mvua* (there was no rain). *Kulikuwa na* means "there was", the past partner of *kuna*.
And for **"had"**: *nilikuwa na pesa* (I had money then), *hatukuwa na muda* (we didn't have time). It's simply *kuwa* + *na*, with the slot attached to *kuwa*.

sections.title: Hali ya hewa — weather, and why hewa means air

blocks.text: *Hali* (state; condition) + *hewa* (air) = the state of the air, i.e. the weather. Both words are borrowed from Arabic.

Weather sentences almost always use *kuna* or *ni*: *Kuna mvua* (it's raining), *Kuna jua kali* (the sun is blazing), *Leo ni baridi* (it's cold today), *Jana kulikuwa na upepo* (it was windy yesterday). To ask: *Hali ya hewa ikoje leo?*

East Africa has **two** rainy seasons, not one: *masika* (March–May, the long rains) and *vuli* (October–December, the short rains). In between comes *kiangazi*, the hot dry season. People here reckon the seasons by the monsoon winds — the same winds that once carried sailors from Arabia and Gujarat to this coast, and their words along with them.
The sentences below are a story frame you can fill in yourself. They all use the *-li-* slot.

English

blocks.text: Story linkers you need from now on: **kwanza** (first), **kisha** or **halafu** (then), **mwisho** (finally), and **kwa hiyo** (so; therefore). With these, your short sentences instantly sound like a story, not a list.
